newsitem.title: UK: Sterling heads grain trade worries before UK vote.
newsitem.headline: Sterling heads grain trade worries before UK vote.

text.p: As British election campaigning starts, uncertainty in foreign exchange markets is the biggest prompt concern for the UK grain trade.
But after a series of food scares, the longer term issue of how the food sector is regulated also preoccupies industry leaders.
Conservative Prime Minister John Major announced on Monday that Britons would vote on May 1. The main opposition Labour Party has the lead in the opinion polls.
UK food industry leaders want to see more done by the next government, of whatever hue, to bolster shaky consumer confidence in food and the food industry.
Even before the election was announced, the campaign was having an indirect effect on the grain market.
On Monday pre-election nervousness pushed the pound down, and LIFFE grain futures duly rose in sympathy.
The food sectors' problems, notably over BSE, have left the grains sector largely unscathed, although there has been an indirect effect on animal feed use.
But unease lingers that cereals in processed and unprocessed form may not be immune from some unforeseen panic.

"Most of all we want to see consumer confidence in food safety restored and we will be interested in what the parties have to say about it," John Murray of the National Association of British and Irish Millers said.

"Really we want to see the new government, of whatever political colour, working hard to restore public confidence in agriculture and food," Jim Reed, director general of the United Kingdom Agricultural Supply Trade Association said.
"It's perfectly obvious that the public has lost faith in the existing institutions."
Labour proposes a separate Food Standards Agency, designed to counter the long standing accusation that the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food is too producer- oriented.
A spokeswoman for Labour agriculture spokesman Gavin Strang described it as "the central plank of our plans for the machinery of government."

"I believe the case is now unanswerable for a powerful food standards agency which sees its task as being the consumer's champion," Labour leader Tony Blair told the Scottish Labour Party conference on March 7.

At the same conference a scientist charged with drawing up plans for the agency, Professor Philip James, director of the Rowlett Research Institute in Aberdeen, said he did not envisage a body along the lines of the powerful US Food and Drug Administration.
But the current ministry would have to be retained, UKASTA's Reed said. "We have to have a minister, going to meetings in Brussels, who has weight inside his own government."
For the grain trade the effects of pre-election uncertainty on the currency will be the fundamental question.

"We are very sensitive to currency," one senior trader said. He pointed out that sterling's Monday morning jitters ahead of the election announcement had been largely responsible for a 1.45 stg jump in the bellwether May wheat contract at LIFFE.
The grain trade cares a lot less about what happens to currency after the election. By then the UK should have dealt with its 4.2 million tonne wheat surplus.
With the latest sales the UK has already exported approaching 4 million tonnes, so after the end of March, currency will matter a lot less.

UKASTA's Reed was also concerned about the effect of the election campaign on the currency. What politicians say during campaigning can have a "totally unpredictable effect on the pound," he said. "It does create instability."

The effect would be limited by the time of year. "We are getting to the fag end of the season," Reed said. A lot of purchasers were fairly well bought forward, but Reed still hoped politicians would be careful what they say.
The England and Wales National Farmers Union welcomed the opportunity provided by the election run-up to focus on key issues affecting rural areas.
In a statement, it particularly focused on beef, noting that on Thursday it will be a year since the government announced a possible connection between BSE in cattle and the human equivalent CJD.
According to the NFU, there are some 73 seats in England and Wales which are rural in character and which are marginal between two or more political parties.

"It's possibly worth mentioning that there are much bigger international factors affecting agriculture than those levels which remain in the hands of politicians in Westminster," UKASTA's Reed said. The result of a British election could not make a major difference to grains markets.
